claim: Two monkeys performed in a sequential choice task in which they made consecutive, trial-by-trial choices to save (i.e. accumulate) liquid reward until they chose to spend (i.e. consume) the accumulated reward.
source: Two monkeys performed in a sequential choice task in which they made consecutive, trial-by-trial choices to save (i.e. accumulate) liquid reward until they chose to spend (i.e. consume) the accumulated reward (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental task design used in the study.

claim: Accumulation of reward over consecutive save choices depended on the current interest rate.
source: Accumulation of reward over consecutive save choices depended on the current interest rate; pre-trained save cues indicated different interest rates.
evidence: This describes a key parameter of the experimental task design.

claim: The animals were free to produce saving sequences of different lengths, which allowed them to plan their behavior over several trials within a sequence and anticipate final reward amounts.
source: The animals were free to produce saving sequences of different lengths, which allowed them to plan their behavior over several trials within a sequence and anticipate final reward amounts.
evidence: This describes the self-determined nature of the task and its implications for behavioral planning.

claim: Save-spend cues appeared pseudorandomly in left-right positions, preventing action planning before cue onset.
source: Save-spend cues appeared pseudorandomly in left-right positions, preventing action planning before cue onset.
evidence: This describes a control feature of the task design to prevent motor preplanning.

claim: Spend choice probability increased with sequence progress.
source: By design, spend choice probability increased with sequence progress (as each sequence ended with a spend choice).
evidence: This describes a behavioral pattern observed in the task.

claim: The relationship between spend probability and sequence progress varied between interest rate conditions, reflecting the animals' preferences for different sequence lengths.
source: However, the relationship between spend probability and sequence progress varied between interest rate conditions, reflecting the animals' preferences for different sequence lengths (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes how behavioral choices varied with task parameters, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The animals typically preferred shorter sequences when interest was low and preferred longer sequences with higher interest.
source: The animals typically preferred shorter sequences when interest was low (early peak in the probability distribution) and preferred longer sequences with higher interest (later peak; correlation between mean sequence length and interest rates across animals: r = 0.71, p=0.003).
evidence: This describes a behavioral preference pattern with statistical support (correlation r = 0.71, p=0.003).

claim: Key release reaction times shortened with sequence progress, separately for spend and save trials.
source: Key release reaction times shortened with sequence progress, separately for spend and save trials (Figure 1D), which suggested higher motivation in later trials of a sequence.
evidence: This describes a behavioral measure (reaction times) that varied with sequence progress, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The effect of sequence progress on reaction times was significant when controlling for other task-relevant variables including subjective choice values.
source: The effect was significant when controlling for other task-relevant variables including subjective choice values (p<0.001, partial correlation).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for the relationship between sequence progress and reaction times after controlling for confounds.

claim: The relationship between reaction times and sequence progress depended on the final length of each sequence: reaction times declined at a faster rate with the progress of shorter sequences.
source: The relationship between reaction times and sequence progress depended on the final length of each sequence: reaction times declined at a faster rate with the progress of shorter sequences (Figure 1E), indicating that the animals adjusted their motivation according to planned sequence length.
evidence: This describes an interaction between sequence progress and sequence length on reaction times, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the imperative control task, reaction times also decreased with sequence progress depending on anticipated sequence length.
source: In the imperative control task, reaction times also decreased with sequence progress depending on anticipated sequence length (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a similar behavioral pattern in the control task, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The influence of sequence progress on reaction times did not depend on task type, suggesting similar behavioral relevance for sequence progress across tasks.
source: Critically, the influence of sequence progress on reaction times did not depend on task type, suggesting similar behavioral relevance for sequence progress across tasks.
evidence: This is an inference from statistical modeling comparing free choice and imperative tasks.

claim: Both animals followed uncued changes in interest rate.
source: Behavioral data from control tests reported previously (Hernadi et al., 2015) confirmed that saving was adaptive and internally controlled: both animals (i) followed uncued changes in interest rate (R = 0.97, p<0.001; linear regression of mean sequence length on interest rate)
evidence: This cites previously reported behavioral data (Hernadi et al., 2015) with statistical support (R = 0.97, p<0.001).

claim: Both animals maximized reward rate for extreme interest conditions.
source: (ii) maximized reward rate for extreme interest conditions (R = 0.73, p=3.3 × 10−7, linear regression of relative choice frequency on normalized rate of reward return across animals)
evidence: This describes behavioral optimization with statistical support (R = 0.73, p=3.3 × 10−7).

claim: Both animals successfully tracked accumulated reward, shown by interspersed challenge trials offering saved vs. fixed reward amounts.
source: (iii) successfully tracked accumulated reward, shown by interspersed challenge trials offering saved vs. fixed reward amounts (p=5.06 × 10−6, Mann-Whitney test on choice frequencies for fixed reward when it exceeded saved reward).
evidence: This describes a behavioral control test with statistical support (p=5.06 × 10−6, Mann-Whitney test).

claim: The animals' choices were well described by a behavioral model based on the subjective values of save and spend choice options.
source: In addition, the animals' choices were well described by a behavioral model based on the subjective values of save and spend choice options (p<1.0 × 10−16, t-test on regression coefficients for subjective save value and spend value, logistic regression).
evidence: This describes model fitting to behavioral data with statistical support (p<1.0 × 10−16, t-test).

claim: A substantial number of amygdala neurons showed gradually changing neuronal responses over consecutive trials in a sequence.
source: As the animals progressed through the self-determined choice sequences, a substantial number of amygdala neurons showed gradually changing neuronal responses over consecutive trials in a sequence (single linear regression, Equation 2: 194/326 neurons, 59%; multiple stepwise regression, Equation 7: 127/326 neurons, 39%).
evidence: This reports the main neurophysiological finding with quantification (194/326 neurons, 59% for single regression; 127/326 neurons, 39% for multiple regression).

claim: The neuron in Figure 2 showed a phasic response related to sequence progress at the time of choice on each trial.
source: The neuron in Figure 2 showed a phasic response related to sequence progress at the time of choice on each trial.
evidence: This describes a specific example neuron shown in Figure 2.

claim: The activity of the neuron in Figure 2 increased gradually over consecutive trials within a sequence and reset with the start of a new sequence.
source: The activity increased gradually over consecutive trials within a sequence and reset with the start of a new sequence (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the temporal pattern of activity for the example neuron, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The gradual activity in the neuron in Figure 2 occurred specifically in the cue phase and preceding fixation phase.
source: This gradual activity occurred specifically in the cue phase and preceding fixation phase (Figure 2B); it was neither a tonic increase in baseline activity nor a trial outcome response.
evidence: This describes the temporal specificity of the neuronal response, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There were no external cues that could have signaled current trial position in the sequence.
source: Crucially, there were no external cues that could have signaled current trial position; accordingly, the observed activity reflected purely internal tracking of sequence progress.
evidence: This describes a key control feature of the task design and its implication for interpreting neuronal activity.

claim: The graded activity in the neuron in Figure 2 disappeared in the cue phase of the imperative task, when behavior was externally instructed.
source: The graded activity disappeared in the cue phase of the imperative task, when behavior was externally instructed (Figure 2C), confirming the relationship to an internal process.
evidence: This describes a task-specific difference in neuronal activity, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Regression analysis established a linear, trial-by-trial relationship between cue-period activity and sequence progress in the free choice task but not in the imperative task for the neuron in Figure 2.
source: Regression analysis (Equation 2) established a linear, trial-by-trial relationship between cue-period activity and sequence progress in the free choice task (Figure 2D) but not in the imperative task (Figure 2E).
evidence: This describes statistical analysis of the example neuron's activity, shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Sensory stimulation, motor requirements and behavioral reward expectation were matched between free choice and imperative task.
source: Importantly, sensory stimulation, motor requirements and behavioral reward expectation were matched between free choice and imperative task, and random cue positions precluded planning of action sequences.
evidence: This describes control features of the experimental design.

claim: The gradually increasing activity in the neuron in Figure 2 did not reflect sensory evidence accumulation or preparation of a motor response.
source: This suggested that the gradually increasing activity did not reflect sensory evidence accumulation or preparation of a motor response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the task design controls.

claim: Linear regression identified amygdala neurons with progress-related activity in different trial periods.
source: Linear regression (Equation 2) identified amygdala neurons with progress-related activity in different trial periods (Figure 3A,B), including pre-choice periods before the animal indicated its current-trial choice (Figure 3A, left), and post-choice periods before outcome (Figure 3A, middle) and after outcome (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This describes the distribution of progress-related activity across task periods, shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: A significant majority of progress-related activities increased (rather than decreased) over consecutive trials within a sequence.
source: A significant majority of progress-related activities increased (rather than decreased) over consecutive trials within a sequence (Figure 3C; 294/408 responses with positive regression slope, Equation 2, 72%; p=1.0 × 10−19, binomial test).
evidence: This describes a directional bias in the population of progress-related responses with statistical support (294/408 responses, 72%; p=1.0 × 10−19, binomial test), shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The significant majority of neurons showed progress-related activity specifically during free choices compared to the imperative task.
source: Although a fraction of these neurons also showed progress-related activity in the imperative task, the significant majority showed progress-related activity specifically during free choices (Figure 3D; p<0.001, z-test for dependent samples).
evidence: This describes a task-specific difference in the prevalence of progress-related activity with statistical support (p<0.001, z-test), shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At the population level, the strength of neuronal progress coding transiently declined on trials when the animals committed an error and subsequently reappeared on the following trials.
source: Consistent with this observation, at the population level, the strength of neuronal progress coding transiently declined on trials when the animals committed an error (failed to perform a correct saccade or prematurely released the touch key), and subsequently reappeared on the following trials (Figure 3E).
evidence: This describes a relationship between neuronal activity and behavioral performance, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Sliding window regression identified progress activities in 214/326 neurons (65.64%).
source: Sliding window regression identified progress activities in a similar numbers of neurons as the main fixed-window regression (214/326 neurons, 65.64%, Equation 2) and confirmed their occurrence throughout different task periods (Figure 3F).
evidence: This reports results from an alternative analysis method, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The majority of sequence progress activities were phasic responses that occurred transiently at specific task events and subsequently disappeared.
source: The majority of sequence progress activities were phasic responses that occurred transiently at specific task events and subsequently disappeared (Figure 3F), rather than reflecting lasting, tonic modulations in activity.
evidence: This describes the temporal characteristics of progress-related activity, shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Few neuronal responses (27/408, 6.6%) reflected sequence progress in addition to previously described sequence length signals.
source: For example, few neuronal responses (27/408, 6.6%) reflected sequence progress in addition to previously described sequence length signals, suggesting distinct encoding of sequence progress and length.
evidence: This quantifies the overlap between progress and length coding with an interpretation about distinct encoding.

claim: 127 neurons (39% of all recorded neurons) showed relation to sequence progress in the strictest regression model, of which 31 neurons (10%) encoded sequence progress without relation to explicit planning variables or choices.
source: Our strictest regression model included sequence progress in addition to planning variables (sequence value, sequence length, Equation 7) and current-trial save-spend choice. This model identified 127 neurons with relation to sequence progress (39%) of which 31 neurons (10% of all recorded neurons) encoded sequence progress without relation to explicit planning variables or choices, suggesting a significant number of neurons with 'pure' progress activity.
evidence: This reports results from the most stringent statistical model with quantification of 'pure' progress neurons.

claim: 78 neurons (24%) encoded 'pure' planning activities and 112 neurons (34%) encoded 'pure' choice activities.
source: For comparison, 78 neurons (24%) neurons encoded 'pure' planning activities (i.e. not coding choice or progress variables) and 112 neurons (34%) encoded 'pure' choice activities (i.e. not coding planning or progress variables).
evidence: This provides comparative quantification of other types of neuronal coding.

claim: Neurons with progress-related activity occurred in both basolateral and centromedial amygdala regions.
source: Although neurons with progress-related activity occurred in both basolateral and centromedial amygdala regions (Figure 3G), they occurred significantly more frequently in the basolateral amygdala (Figure 3H).
evidence: This describes the anatomical distribution of progress neurons, shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: Progress neurons occurred significantly more frequently in the basolateral amygdala compared to centromedial amygdala.
source: Although neurons with progress-related activity occurred in both basolateral and centromedial amygdala regions (Figure 3G), they occurred significantly more frequently in the basolateral amygdala (Figure 3H).
evidence: This describes a regional difference in the prevalence of progress neurons, shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The neuron in Figure 4A–B showed neuronal adaptation where during short sequences of less than five trials, progress activity rose steeply from baseline to a maximum of about 40 Hz, whereas for longer sequences, activity increased at a much lower rate.
source: The neuron in Figure 4A–B, showed exactly this kind of neuronal adaptation. During short sequences of less than five trials, progress activity rose steeply from baseline to a maximum of about 40 Hz (regression slope from unbinned data, Equation 2: 7.33), whereas for longer sequences, activity increased at a much lower rate (slope: 2.14).
evidence: This describes adaptive coding in an example neuron with quantified slopes (7.33 vs. 2.14), shown in Figures 4A-B.

claim: At the population level, increases in activity with sequence progress were steep for short sequences and successively shallower for longer sequences.
source: As for the single neuron, increases in population activity with sequence progress were steep for short sequences and successively shallower for longer sequences (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This describes adaptive coding at the population level, shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: There was a linear positive relationship between the rate of activity increase (population progress slope) and inverse sequence length.
source: This was quantified by a linear positive relationship between the rate of activity increase (population progress slope) and inverse sequence length (Figure 4E).
evidence: This quantifies the adaptive relationship at the population level, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The rate of activity increase adapted to the length of the current choice sequence, consistent with principles of adaptive coding.
source: Thus, the rate of activity increase adapted to the length of the current choice sequence, consistent with principles of adaptive coding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neuronal data in relation to coding theory.

claim: Choice sequence lengths were internally planned rather than externally instructed, which implied prospective neuronal adaptation to an internally planned parameter.
source: Crucially, choice sequence lengths were internally planned rather than externally instructed, which implied prospective neuronal adaptation to an internally planned parameter.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the neuronal adaptation based on the task design.

claim: Progress-related activity at specific sequence steps allowed prediction of the forthcoming sequence lengths, as early as the second trial of a sequence.
source: Confirming a prospective adaptation, progress-related activity at specific sequence steps allowed prediction of the forthcoming sequence lengths, as early as the second trial of a sequence (Figure 4F).
evidence: This describes predictive information in neuronal activity, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The predictive effect of progress-related activity on sequence length was found for all sequence steps except first sequence trials.
source: This effect was found for all sequence steps (all p<0.001, linear regression) except first sequence trials (p=0.26), which implied a constant starting point of progress activity in each sequence.
evidence: This describes the temporal specificity of the predictive relationship with statistical support (all p<0.001 except first trial p=0.26).

claim: After a steep activity increase during two-trial sequences, activity increase was much shallower during immediately following five-trial sequences.
source: After a steep activity increase during two-trial sequences, activity increase was much shallower during immediately following five-trial sequences (Figure 4G).
evidence: This describes rapid adaptation in population activity across consecutive sequences, shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The rapid downward adaption of progress slope reversed when sequential order was reversed, i.e. when a two-trial sequence followed a five-trial sequence.
source: This rapid downward adaption of progress slope reversed when sequential order was reversed, i.e. when a two-trial sequence followed a five-trial sequence (Figure 4H).
evidence: This describes bidirectional adaptation in population activity, shown in Figure 4H.

claim: There was a significant regression of the (signed) progress activity slope difference on the (signed) difference in sequence length across all pairs of consecutive saving sequences.
source: We quantified this dynamic adaptation across all pairs of consecutive saving sequences by a significant regression of the (signed) progress activity slope difference on the (signed) difference in sequence length (Figure 4I).
evidence: This quantifies the dynamic adaptation across consecutive sequences, shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The adaptive progress model explained a higher number of responses than a non-adaptive progress model (447 vs. 408 significant responses).
source: Linear regression revealed that this adaptive progress model explained a higher number of responses than a non-adaptive progress model (447 vs. 408 significant responses, Equation 3 vs. Equation 2), with a significantly higher number of best fits (391 vs. 104 responses with higher R2 for adaptive model; p<1.0 × 10−23, z-test for dependent samples).
evidence: This reports model comparison results with statistical support (p<1.0 × 10−23, z-test).

claim: Across all responses that were significant for both adaptive and non-adaptive models, the R2 distribution was shifted significantly towards the adaptive model.
source: Across all responses that were significant for both models, the R2 distribution was shifted significantly towards the adaptive model (Figure 5B, left) and the R2 difference between models was significantly in favor of the adaptive model (p=3.2 × 10−8, one-sample t-test).
evidence: This describes the distribution of model fits with statistical support (p=3.2 × 10−8, one-sample t-test), shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The adaptive sequence progress model proved superior to models based on accumulated reward magnitude, elapsed time, and tuning to specific sequence steps.
source: The adaptive sequence progress model also proved superior to other alternatives (Figure 5A–B), including models based on the accumulated reward magnitude (saved juice, Equation 4), elapsed time (incorporating error trials, Equation 5), and tuning to specific sequence steps (Equation 6, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This reports comprehensive model comparisons, shown in Figures 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all model comparisons, the adaptive progress model explained a higher number of responses, with a significantly higher number of best fits (all p<1.0 × 10−20, z-test for dependent samples), and with significant shifts in R2 distribution towards the adaptive model (all p<1.0 × 10−7, one-sample t-test).
source: In all cases, the adaptive progress model explained a higher number of responses, with a significantly higher number of best fits (all p<1.0 × 10−20, z-test for dependent samples), and with significant shifts in R2 distribution towards the adaptive model (all p<1.0 × 10−7, one-sample t-test).
evidence: This summarizes statistical support for the adaptive model across multiple comparisons.

claim: A partial adaptation model provided a better fit to the data than the non-adaptive model.
source: The partial adaptation model was also motivated by related approaches in economics (Koszegi and Rabin, 2006) that model dependence of individuals' preferences on external reference points using partial adaptation, although with different formalisms. Similar to the full adaptive model, a partial adaptation provided a better fit to the data than the non-adaptive model (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This reports model comparison results with reference to economic theory (Koszegi and Rabin, 2006), shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: On average both full adaptation and partial adaptation fit the data equally well.
source: However, even though some individual responses were better explained by partial adaptation compared to full adaptation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), and aspects of population activity seemed more consistent with partial adaptation (Figure 4C), on average both full adaptation and partial adaptation fit the data equally well (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) and explained similar numbers of responses (full adaptive model: 447/1126 task-related responses, 39.7%; partial adaptive model: 435/1126 responses, 38.6%).
evidence: This compares full and partial adaptation models with quantification, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G and Figure 4C.

claim: In the imperative task, the adaptive progress model did not explain a higher number of responses and did not have a higher number of best-fit responses compared with the main alternative models.
source: True to this prediction, in the imperative task, the adaptive progress model did not explain a higher number of responses and did not have a higher number of best-fit responses compared with the main alternative models (p>0.1).
evidence: This reports model comparison results for the imperative task with statistical support (p>0.1).

claim: The relative advantage of the adaptive model was significantly larger in the free choice task compared to the imperative task in all cases except for the tuning model.
source: Directly contrasting model fits between free and imperative tasks showed that the relative advantage of the adaptive model (quantified by positive R2 difference between models) was significantly larger in the free choice task compared to the imperative task in all cases (Figure 5D), except for the tuning model, which was similarly inferior in both tasks (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This compares model performance across tasks, shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activity in some neurons reflected trial-by-trial reaction times (saccadic reaction times: 55/326 neurons, 17%; 65/1126 task-related responses, 6%; key reaction times: 82/326 neurons, 25%; 105/1126 task-related responses, 9%).
source: Similar to previous studies (Peck and Salzman, 2014), activity in some neurons reflected trial-by-trial reaction times (saccadic reaction times: 55/326 neurons, 17%; 65/1126 task-related responses, 6%; key reaction times: 82/326 neurons, 25%; 105/1126 task-related responses, 9%).
evidence: This reports relationships between neuronal activity and reaction times with citation to previous work (Peck and Salzman, 2014).

claim: Neuronal responses related to reaction times were more frequent in centromedial than in basolateral amygdala neurons.
source: Neuronal responses related to reaction times were more frequent in centromedial than in basolateral amygdala neurons (saccade reaction times: 38 vs. 27; key reaction times: 59 vs. 46; both p<0.005; χ²-test).
evidence: This describes a regional difference in reaction time coding with statistical support (both p<0.005; χ²-test).

claim: Accounting for reaction times did not explain the main result of neuronal responses related to sequence progress.
source: Importantly, accounting for reaction times did not explain our main result of neuronal responses related to sequence progress: the stepwise regression with reaction times as covariates identified 176 neuronal responses (15%) in 117 neurons (36%) related to sequence progress.
evidence: This reports control analysis results showing that progress coding persists after accounting for reaction times.

claim: Cross-validated decoding performance of a nearest-neighbor classifier was significantly above chance in all trial phases with mean accuracy of 78.13 ± 0.56%.
source: Cross-validated decoding performance of a nearest-neighbor classifier (Quian Quiroga et al., 2006) was significantly above chance in all trial phases (Figure 6A; mean accuracy: 78.13 ± 0.56%) with maximum accuracy of 89% in the fixation phase.
evidence: This reports population decoding results with citation (Quian Quiroga et al., 2006), shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Decoding performance increased steadily with the number of neurons used for decoding, which suggested that different neurons contributed partly independent information.
source: Decoding performance increased steadily with the number of neurons used for decoding (Figure 6B), which suggested that different neurons contributed partly independent information.
evidence: This describes how decoding accuracy scaled with population size with an interpretation about independence, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Considerable information about sequence progress was present in amygdala neurons during the imperative task, even though decoding was on average better during the free choice task.
source: Interestingly, comparing decoding between free choice and imperative task for neurons recorded in both tasks shows that considerable information about sequence progress was present in amygdala neurons during the imperative task, even though decoding was on average better during the free choice task (Figure 6B inset; p=0.033, Wilcoxon test on accuracies for maximum number for neurons shown in Figure 6B inset).
evidence: This compares decoding performance across tasks with statistical support (p=0.033, Wilcoxon test), shown in Figure 6B inset.

claim: Decoding based on small subsets of randomly selected neurons was well above chance.
source: Decoding based on these small subsets of randomly selected neurons was well above chance (Figure 6D, 'Random').
evidence: This reports subset decoding results, shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Even individually non-significant neurons contributed to decoding.
source: This suggested that even individually non-significant neurons contributed to decoding (Figure 6D, 'N-signif').
evidence: This is an inference from the subset decoding analysis, shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Decoding performance depended strongly on individual neurons' sensitivities (slopes) to sequence progress.
source: Overall, however, decoding performance depended strongly on individual neurons' sensitivities (slopes) to sequence progress (Figure 6E).
evidence: This describes a relationship between single-neuron properties and population decoding, shown in Figure 6E.

claim: For both basolateral and centromedial regions, decoding was well above chance in all task periods.
source: For both regions, decoding was well above chance in all task periods (Figure 6F).
evidence: This reports regional decoding results, shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In the fixation period, decoding performance was significantly higher for basolateral neurons, whereas in the cue period performance was significantly higher for centromedial neurons.
source: Notably, in the fixation period, decoding performance was significantly higher for basolateral neurons, whereas in the cue period performance was significantly higher for centromedial neurons (Figure 6F).
evidence: This describes task period-specific regional differences in decoding, shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In the fixation period, adding more neurons increased performance for both basolateral and centromedial neurons, with overall higher accuracy for basolateral neurons.
source: In the fixation period, adding more neurons increased performance for both basolateral and centromedial neurons, with overall higher accuracy for basolateral neurons (Figure 6G).
evidence: This describes how decoding scaled with population size for different regions in the fixation period, shown in Figure 6G.

claim: In the cue period, accuracy increased substantially as more centromedial neurons were added, with significantly lower accuracy increases for basolateral neurons.
source: By contrast, in the cue period, accuracy increased substantially as more centromedial neurons were added, with significantly lower accuracy increases for basolateral neurons (Figure 6H).
evidence: This describes how decoding scaled with population size for different regions in the cue period, shown in Figure 6H.

claim: In the fixation period, the relative number of centromedial neurons in a decoding subset had no impact on performance.
source: In the fixation period, the relative number of centromedial neurons in a decoding subset had no impact on performance (Figure 6I).
evidence: This reports subset analysis results for the fixation period, shown in Figure 6I.

claim: In the cue phase, adding more centromedial neurons (relative to basolateral neurons) significantly increased decoding accuracy, even irrespective of their progress sensitivities.
source: By contrast, in the cue phase, adding more centromedial neurons (relative to basolateral neurons) significantly increased decoding accuracy, even irrespective of their progress sensitivities, which were covariates in the analysis (Figure 6J).
evidence: This reports subset analysis results for the cue period, shown in Figure 6J.

claim: The amygdala is a prime valuation structure.
source: The amygdala is a prime valuation structure yet its functions in advanced behaviors are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about amygdala function based on established knowledge.

claim: The functions of the amygdala in advanced behaviors are poorly understood.
source: The amygdala is a prime valuation structure yet its functions in advanced behaviors are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Amygdala neurons showed phasic, gradually increasing responses over successive choice steps as monkeys progressed through choice sequences toward rewards.
source: As monkeys progressed through choice sequences toward rewards, amygdala neurons showed phasic, gradually increasing responses over successive choice steps.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: The gradually increasing responses occurred in the absence of external progress cues or motor preplanning.
source: These responses occurred in the absence of external progress cues or motor preplanning.
evidence: This describes key control features of the task that constrain interpretation of the neuronal responses.

claim: The gradually increasing responses were often specific to self-defined sequences, typically disappearing during instructed control sequences with similar reward expectation.
source: They were often specific to self-defined sequences, typically disappearing during instructed control sequences with similar reward expectation.
evidence: This describes task-specificity of the neuronal responses.

claim: The build-up rate of the gradually increasing responses reflected prospectively the forthcoming choice sequence, suggesting adaptation to an internal plan.
source: Their build-up rate reflected prospectively the forthcoming choice sequence, suggesting adaptation to an internal plan.
evidence: This describes adaptive properties of the neuronal responses with an interpretation about internal planning.

claim: Population decoding demonstrated a high-accuracy progress code.
source: Population decoding demonstrated a high-accuracy progress code.
evidence: This summarizes the population decoding results.

claim: Amygdala neurons evaluate the progress of planned, self-defined behavioral sequences.
source: These findings indicate that amygdala neurons evaluate the progress of planned, self-defined behavioral sequences.
evidence: This is the main interpretive conclusion of the study.

claim: Progress signals seem essential for aligning stepwise choices with internal plans.
source: Such progress signals seem essential for aligning stepwise choices with internal plans.
evidence: This is an interpretation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The presence of progress signals in amygdala neurons may inform understanding of human conditions with amygdala dysfunction and deregulated reward pursuit.
source: Their presence in amygdala neurons may inform understanding of human conditions with amygdala dysfunction and deregulated reward pursuit.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical implications.

claim: The amygdala is a nuclear complex in the medial temporal lobe.
source: The amygdala, a nuclear complex in the medial temporal lobe, is a key structure for the internal evaluation of sensory events (Janak and Tye, 2015; LeDoux, 2000; Morrison and Salzman, 2010; Murray and Rudebeck, 2013; Rolls, 2000).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by multiple citations.

claim: The amygdala is a key structure for the internal evaluation of sensory events.
source: The amygdala, a nuclear complex in the medial temporal lobe, is a key structure for the internal evaluation of sensory events (Janak and Tye, 2015; LeDoux, 2000; Morrison and Salzman, 2010; Murray and Rudebeck, 2013; Rolls, 2000).
evidence: This is a functional characterization supported by multiple citations (Janak and Tye, 2015; LeDoux, 2000; Morrison and Salzman, 2010; Murray and Rudebeck, 2013; Rolls, 2000).

claim: The amygdala has a classical role in fear conditioning.
source: In addition to the classical role in fear conditioning (Duvarci and Pare, 2014; LeDoux, 2000; Namburi et al., 2015; Paz and Pare, 2013), amygdala neurons also respond to reward, encode stimulus-reward associations and signal reward expectation
evidence: This is a well-established function supported by multiple citations (Duvarci and Pare, 2014; LeDoux, 2000; Namburi et al., 2015; Paz and Pare, 2013).

claim: Amygdala neurons respond to reward, encode stimulus-reward associations and signal reward expectation.
source: amygdala neurons also respond to reward, encode stimulus-reward associations and signal reward expectation (Belova et al., 2007; Bermudez and Schultz, 2010; Bermudez et al., 2012; Namburi et al., 2015; Nishijo et al., 1988; Paton et al., 2006; Rolls, 2000; Schoenbaum et al., 1998; Schultz, 2015; Shabel and Janak, 2009).
evidence: This describes reward-related functions supported by multiple citations (Belova et al., 2007; Bermudez and Schultz, 2010; Bermudez et al., 2012; Namburi et al., 2015; Nishijo et al., 1988; Paton et al., 2006; Rolls, 2000; Schoenbaum et al., 1998; Schultz, 2015; Shabel and Janak, 2009).

claim: A central, integrative valuation role is compatible with the amygdala's extensive sensory and prefrontal connections, its outputs to attentional, autonomic, and behavioral control systems, and its processing of social cues.

claim: Advanced economic behaviors often require sequences of choices organized by an internal plan.
source: Advanced economic behaviors often require sequences of choices organized by an internal plan.

claim: In economic saving, the plan to obtain a reward in the future guides sequential choices and actions in the present.
source: In economic saving, for example, the plan to obtain a reward in the future guides sequential choices and actions in the present (Benhabib and Bisin, 2005).
evidence: This is an example from economic theory supported by a citation (Benhabib and Bisin, 2005).

claim: A critical requirement during planned choice sequences is the continual evaluation of progress, to ensure alignment of individual choices with long-term plans and successful navigation toward reward goals.
source: A critical requirement during planned choice sequences is the continual evaluation of progress, to ensure alignment of individual choices with long-term plans and successful navigation toward reward goals (Benhabib and Bisin, 2005; Berkman and Lieberman, 2009; Johnson and Busemeyer, 2001).

claim: During externally instructed, multistep reward schedules, neurons in frontal cortex, amygdala and striatum respond to cues signaling schedule onset, reward contingency and reward proximity.
source: Furthermore, during externally instructed, multistep reward schedules, neurons in frontal cortex, amygdala and striatum respond to cues signaling schedule onset, reward contingency and reward proximity (Shidara and Richmond, 2002; Simmons et al., 2007; Sugase-Miyamoto and Richmond, 2005).

claim: Previous studies uncovered important neural components of externally instructed sequential behaviors but did not address the internal progress evaluation that is typical of economic choice plans toward self-defined goals.
source: These studies uncovered important neural components of externally instructed sequential behaviors but did not address the internal progress evaluation that is typical of economic choice plans toward self-defined goals.

claim: The amygdala's diverse anatomical connections would make a sequence progress signal widely available for cognitive, motivational and behavioral computation in different downstream neurons.
source: Its diverse anatomical connections would make a sequence progress signal widely available for cognitive, motivational and behavioral computation in different downstream neurons.

claim: Amygdala dysfunction occurs in humans with deregulated reward pursuit and affective disorders.

evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by citations (Koob and Volkow, 2010; Price and Drevets, 2010).

claim: Amygdala dysfunction impacts on the motivation to plan for and pursue distant rewards.

claim: Previously reported amygdala neurons signal immediate, current-trial choices.
source: Previously, we reported prospective amygdala signaling of immediate, current-trial choices (Grabenhorst et al., 2012) and forthcoming choice sequences (Hernadi et al., 2015).

evidence: This cites previous work by the authors (Hernadi et al., 2015).

claim: Signals for immediate choices and forthcoming sequences cannot by themselves guide stepwise choices toward a final reward goal.
source: Although such signals are essential for internally planned behavior, they cannot by themselves guide stepwise choices toward a final reward goal.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of previously described signals.

claim: Gradual amygdala responses evolved dynamically during internally planned choice sequences lasting up to two minutes.
source: In the present study, we report gradually increasing amygdala responses that evolved dynamically during internally planned choice sequences lasting up to two minutes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding with temporal quantification.

claim: Gradual amygdala responses were mostly specific to free, internally guided choices as they typically disappeared in externally instructed sequences, despite similar behavioral reward expectation.
source: The gradual amygdala responses were mostly specific to free, internally guided choices as they typically disappeared in externally instructed sequences, despite similar behavioral reward expectation.
evidence: This describes task-specificity of the neuronal responses.

claim: The gradual build-up rate of amygdala responses readily adapted to the forthcoming, internally planned choice sequence length, suggesting reference to an internal plan.
source: Importantly, their gradual build-up rate readily adapted to the forthcoming, internally planned choice sequence length, suggesting reference to an internal plan.
evidence: This describes adaptive properties of the neuronal responses with an interpretation about internal planning.

claim: The neuronal population provided a highly accurate progress code.
source: Decoding analysis showed that the neuronal population provided a highly accurate progress code.
evidence: This summarizes the population decoding results.

claim: Primate amygdala neurons encode internally evaluated progress during planned economic choice sequences.
source: These data suggest that primate amygdala neurons encode internally evaluated progress during planned economic choice sequences.
evidence: This is the main interpretive conclusion of the study.

claim: Gradual activity in amygdala neurons seems suited to support multistep decision-making and motivational regulation during the pursuit of self-defined distant rewards.
source: Such gradual activity seems suited to support multistep decision-making and motivational regulation during the pursuit of self-defined distant rewards.
evidence: This is an interpretation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Two adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta), weighing 9.2 and 12.0 kg, participated in the present experiments.
source: Two adult male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta), weighing 9.2 and 12.0 kg, participated in the present experiments.

evidence: This is a statement about methodological standards in the field.

claim: Single-neuron activity was recorded extracellularly from dorsal, lateral, and basal amygdala.
source: We recorded single-neuron activity extracellularly, using standard electrophysiological techniques, from dorsal, lateral, and basal amygdala.
evidence: This describes the recording methods and anatomical targets.

claim: In exploratory tests, activity was sampled from about 700 amygdala neurons.
source: In exploratory tests, we sampled activity from about 700 amygdala neurons and recorded and saved the activity of neurons that appeared to respond to any task event during online inspection of several trials.
evidence: This describes the initial sampling procedure.

source: This procedure resulted in a database of 326 neurons which we analyzed statistically.

source: The number of neurons is similar to those reported in previous studies on primate amygdala.

claim: Monkeys chose on each trial to save (accumulate) the liquid reward that was available on that trial, which increased its magnitude by a variable 'interest rate', or spend (consume) the saved amount.
source: Monkeys chose on each trial to save (accumulate) the liquid reward that was available on that trial, which increased its magnitude by a variable 'interest rate', or spend (consume) the saved amount.
evidence: This describes the basic task structure.

claim: Increase in reward magnitude over sequential save choices were governed by a geometric series.
source: Increase in reward magnitude over sequential save choices were governed by a geometric series (Equation 1)
evidence: This describes the mathematical relationship governing reward accumulation.

claim: Choice sequences were self-determined in that monkeys were free to produce save-spend sequences of different lengths.
source: Choice sequences were self-determined in that monkeys were free to produce save-spend sequences of different lengths (following one required save choice per sequence).
evidence: This describes the self-determined nature of the task.

claim: For high interest rates, a fixed amount of 8 ml was delivered after seven consecutive save trials, as this was the maximum amount the animals could consume on one trial.
source: For high interest rates, we delivered a fixed amount of 8 ml after seven consecutive save trials, as this was the maximum amount the animals could consume on one trial.
evidence: This describes a constraint in the task design based on the animals' consumption capacity.

claim: After training, the animals only generated sequences that resulted in reward amounts that they could comfortably drink.
source: After training, the animals only generated sequences that resulted in reward amounts that they could comfortably drink.
evidence: This describes a behavioral pattern after training.

claim: A critical task parameter for the animals was the number of completed trials since the start of the current saving choice sequence, termed 'sequence progress'.
source: A critical task parameter for the animals was the number of completed trials since the start of the current saving choice sequence. This parameter, which we term 'sequence progress', evolved dynamically within a sequence and thus determined both reward proximity and accumulated reward amount (Equation 1).
evidence: This defines a key variable in the study.

claim: Sequence progress evolved dynamically within a sequence and thus determined both reward proximity and accumulated reward amount.
source: This parameter, which we term 'sequence progress', evolved dynamically within a sequence and thus determined both reward proximity and accumulated reward amount (Equation 1).
evidence: This describes the properties and significance of sequence progress.

claim: Neither free choice task nor imperative control task provided external cues about how many trials had been completed within a sequence, requiring the animals to track progress internally.
source: Crucially, neither free choice task nor imperative control task provided external cues about how many trials had been completed within a sequence, requiring the animals to track progress internally.
evidence: This describes a key control feature of the task design.

claim: The animals were overtrained by the time of neuronal recording and showed consistent, meaningful saving behavior for different interest rates without further signs of learning.
source: The animals were overtrained by the time of neuronal recording and showed consistent, meaningful saving behavior for different interest rates without further signs of learning.
evidence: This describes the training state of the animals during recordings.

claim: In the imperative control task, the animals performed behavioral sequences of matched lengths to the free choice task.
source: In the imperative control task, the animals performed behavioral sequences of matched lengths to the free choice task.

claim: In the imperative control task, the behavior was not self-controlled but was externally instructed by a small visual cue presented next to either the save or the spend cue.
source: However, the behavior was not self-controlled but was externally instructed by a small visual cue presented next to either the save or the spend cue.

source: We matched the ratio of save to spend trials between imperative and free choice task for each monkey and interest rate to allow the animals to anticipate reward amounts which we confirmed by behavioral reaction times (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The imperative task was performed for a subset of recorded neurons in a separate trial block.
source: The imperative task was performed for a subset of recorded neurons in a separate trial block.

claim: For neurons tested in both tasks, the tasks were on average counterbalanced so that either the free choice or imperative task was recorded first.
source: For these neurons, the tasks were on average counterbalanced so that either the free choice or imperative task was recorded first.

claim: Mean sequence lengths were highly correlated between pairs of free choice and imperative sessions (R = 0.527, p=2.1 × 10−12).
source: However, this is unlikely to be a major factor in our results as mean sequence lengths were highly correlated between pairs of free choice and imperative sessions (R = 0.527, p=2.1 × 10−12) and sequence length ranges did not differ significantly on average (p=0.949, t-test).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for matching between tasks (R = 0.527, p=2.1 × 10−12).
